newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: FEATURE - Malnutrition could cost Bangladesh $22 bln.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Malnutrition could cost Bangladesh $22 bln.

text.p: Poor and overpopulated Bangladesh can expect to suffer $22 billion in economic losses over the next decade unless it steps up the fight against malnutrition, World Bank officials said.

"We are losing our productivity due to severe lack of nutrition. People are becoming shorter and losing work capacity," said Dr A.F.M. Iqbal Kabir, a nutrition specialist and programme officer with the World Bank.

"The country's economy will lose $22.4 billion in the next 10 years if we fail to improve our nutrition situation," he said, quoting from a nutrition profile prepared by the U.N. International Children's Emergency Fund (UNICEF).
Alam, a Bangladeshi, was speaking to journalists on a trip to a World Bank-sponsored child feeding centre at Shaharasti in Chandpur district, southeast of Dhaka.
A CRITICAL PROBLEM
"Malnutrition is a critically serious problem in Bangladesh. Between 35-50 percent of new-born babies are below normal weight (less than 2,500 grams)," Alam said.
"About 700 children die every day due to nutrition deficiency. About 70 percent of mothers and children suffer from anaemia caused by iron-deficiency."
Alam said: "Malnutrition leads to a great health hazard ...and adversely affects physical growth, mental capacity, learning ability and productivity."

The Shaharasti feeding centre is part of the Bangladesh Integrated Nutrition Project (BINP), where 33 severely malnourished children receive supplementary food daily. Another baby died shortly after the centre was opened on November 13.

"The baby was severely malnourished and we were just helpless," said Mukti Shaha, a field supervisor of the Bangladesh Rural Advancement Committee (BRAC), a non-government organisation helping the joint Bangladesh-World Bank effort against malnutrition.
She said children brought to the centre are under two years old. They will be fed for two years before a detailed "progress review" will be done.
EXPANSION PLANS

Shaharasti is the first of six such centres to be opened across Bangladesh over the next two years. The World Bank will provide $59.8 million of the $67.3 million project. The Bangladesh government will fund the rest.
If progress in the six centres is satisfactory, the number would be gradually expanded to 40, World Bank officials said.
Anjuman Ara Begum, a mother of two, comes to the Shaharasti centre six days a week to get her nine-month-old second child a supplementary diet -- a paste of rice, pulse, molasses and soyabean oil.
LACK OF AWARENESS
"They are not all poor, but they are ignorant that their babies are suffering from acute malnutrition," Shaha said.
The situation is no better in the Shaharasti police station area, where the literacy rate is 43 percent, compared to a national average of 37 percent, officials said.
About 14 million of the 16 million Bangladeshi children under age five are malnourished, UNICEF officials said.
Up to 20,000 women die annually due to pregnancy-related problems, a quarter of them anaemia, they said.

Bangladesh's population is around 120 million. Per capita income is $230. According to official estimates, more than 50 percent of the population lives below the poverty level, consuming less than 1,800 calories per day.
DEVELOPING A NATIONAL PROGRAMME
Due to the problems, the Bangladeshi government undertook the BINP, in which the World Bank is principal financier, UNICEF provides technical assistance and the BRAC acts as facilitator.

General project objectives are to develop a comprehensive national programme to reduce malnutrition, particularly among women and children, "by ensuring household food security, behavioural changes about food intake and growth monitoring", BINP officials said.
The specific objective was to reduce by half severe malnutrition among children under five, they said but gave no time frame.
